5. Reflection and Refraction

Subject: MOC - physics

Content

LIGHT

  • Light is defined as a form of electromagnetic radiation, specifically the part of the electromagnetic spectrum that is visible to the human eye.
  • Light has dual nature (Light exhibits both wave-like and particle-like characteristics).
  • Light can also be described as a stream of particles called photons, which carry energy.
  • Light travels at a constant speed in a vacuum, approx. 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
  • Light is a form of transverse wave that travels in vacuum.
  • Light can be polarized.

Young's Double-Slit Experiment

  • It was performed in 1801 by Thomas Young, demonstrates the wave-like nature of light, showing that light can interfere with itself, creating an interference pattern of bright and dark fringes.

Photoelectric Effect

  • The photoelectric effect is a phenomenon where electrons are emitted from the metal surface when light of sufficient frequency is incident upon it.
  • This effect led to the conclusion that light is made up of packets or quantum of energy.
  • Heinrich Rudolf Hertz was the first to observe the photoelectric effect in 1887.
  • In 1905, Albert Einstein proposed the existence of photons, discrete packets of energy, to explain the photoelectric effect and other light-related phenomena (received Nobel Prize in 1921).

Reflection of Light

  • Reflection occurs when light rays strike a surface and change direction, returning to the same medium instead of passing through or being absorbed.

Laws of Reflection

  1. 1. The angle of incidence (i) is equal to the angle of reflection (r).
  2. 2. The incident ray, reflected ray, and the normal all lie in the same plane.

SPHERICAL MIRRORS

There are different types of mirrors and they are broadly classified as:

→ Plane Mirrors, Concave Mirrors, Convex Mirror.

TypeDescriptionImage Nature
Plane MirrorFlat mirrorVirtual, erect, laterally inverted
Concave MirrorReflecting surface curves inwardReal/Inverted or Virtual/Erect depending on object position
Convex MirrorReflecting surface curves outwardAlways Virtual, erect, and diminished

Types of Image

Images are classified as either real or virtual, based on whether light rays actually converge to form the image, or only appear to diverge from a point.

Real ImageVirtual Image
Can be projected on a screenCannot be projected on a screen
Formed when light rays actually converge and intersect after reflection or refractionFormed when light rays appear to diverge from a point, but do not actually intersect
Always inverted (upside down)Always upright (right side up)
Formed by concave mirrors and convex lensesFormed by convex mirrors, concave lenses, and plane mirrors
Real objects are points from which light diverges. Virtual objects are points towards which light converges.

Image Formation in Plane Mirror

  • Virtual Image: The image cannot be projected onto a screen and is formed behind the mirror.
  • Erect Image: The image is upright (not inverted), i.e., it has the same orientation as the object.
  • Lateral Inversion: The left and right sides of the object appear interchanged in the image.
  • Same Size: The image and object have the same size.
  • Equal Distances: The distance between the object and the mirror is equal to the distance between the image and the mirror.

Image Formation by Concave Mirror

  • A concave mirror can form both real and virtual images.
Object PositionImage PositionNatureImage Size
At infinityAt focusReal, invertedHighly diminished
Beyond CBetween C & FReal, invertedDiminished
At CAt CReal, invertedSame size
Between C & FBeyond CReal, invertedEnlarged
At FAt infinityReal, invertedHighly enlarged
Between F & PBehind mirrorVirtual, erectEnlarged

Legend: C = Curvature, F = Focus, P = Pole

Image Formation by Convex Mirror (Diverging in Nature)

  • A convex mirror forms an image that is always virtual, erect, and diminished (regardless of the object's position) and appears behind the mirror.
Object PositionImage PositionNatureImage Size
At infinityAt F, behind the mirrorVirtual, erectHighly diminished, point-sized
Between infinity and P of the mirrorBetween P and F, behind the mirrorVirtual, erectDiminished

Sign Convention in Spherical Mirror

  • All distances are measured from the pole of the mirror.
  • Distances to the right of the pole are considered positive.
  • Distances to the left of the pole are considered negative.
  • Distances above the principal axis are considered positive.
  • Distances below the principal axis are considered negative.
Focal length of concave mirror is always Negative; Focal length of convex mirror is always Positive.

In Spherical Mirrors

  • Object Distance (u): Always negative (since the object is placed in front of the mirror).
  • Image Distance (v):
  • → Concave mirror: Real image (v is negative) and virtual image (v is positive).
  • → Convex mirror: Image is always virtual and v is positive.
  • Focal Length (f): Concave mirror (f is negative) and convex mirror (f is positive).
  • Radius of Curvature (R): Same sign as focal length (R = 2f).

Mirror Formula

1/v + 1/u = 1/f
Magnification of Mirrors = hi/ho = -v/u

Interpretation of M:

  • M = 2 (image size is twice the size of an object)
  • M = -2 (image is real and inverted)
  • M = 0.2 (image size is smaller than the object)

Worked Example:

An object 4.0 cm in size, is placed 25.0 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15.0 cm. At what distance from the mirror should a screen be placed in order to obtain a sharp image? Find the nature and the size of the image.

Sol: Given — Object height (ho) = 4.0 cm; Object distance (u) = -25.0 cm (object is in front → negative); Focal length (f) = -15.0 cm (concave mirror → negative).

Using 1/v + 1/u = 1/f: 1/v - 1/15 = 1/25 → 1/v + 1/25 - 1/15 = -2/75 → v = -37.5 cm

M = v/u = -37.5/-25 = 1.5; Image Height (hi) = M × ho = 1.5 × 4 = 6 cm.

Uses of Spherical Mirrors

  • Concave Mirror: Shaving and dentist mirrors, car headlights, telescopes, solar furnace, etc.
  • Convex Mirror: Rear view mirrors in vehicles, security monitors in ATMs and stores, surveillance mirrors, sunglasses, etc.

Refraction of Light

  • The refraction of light is the bending of light rays as they pass from one medium to another, thereby causing a change in its speed and direction. Refraction occurs due to a change in the speed of the light ray or wave.
  • While the speed and wavelength of light changes as it moves into a different medium, the frequency, which is determined by the light source, remains constant.
  • This bending by refraction makes it possible for us to have lenses, magnifying glasses, prisms and rainbows.

Laws of Refraction

  1. 1. The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence: All lie in the same plane.
  2. 2. The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence (i) and sine of the angle of refraction (r) is constant (also known as Snell's Law).
Sin i (Angle of Incidence) / Sin r (Angle of Refraction) = Constant = μ

where μ (mu) is the refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first.

Light has rectilinear motion (moves in a straight line).

Refractive Index (μ)

μ = Speed of light in vacuum / Speed of light in medium

Types of Medium

  1. 1. Rare Medium: Light bends away from the normal when moving from a denser to a rarer medium.
  2. 2. Denser Medium: Light bends toward the normal when moving from a rarer to a denser medium.

Let's Take a Look At Three Cases

  • Case A: Same Medium (No Refraction): When light travels through two mediums with the same optical density (E.g., air to air or water to water), it continues in a straight line without bending. This is because the speed of light remains constant, and there's no change in the direction of the light ray.
  • → Case B: From Rarer to Denser Medium: When light travels from a rarer medium to a denser medium (E.g., air to glass or water), it bends towards the normal (the line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence). <i is greater than r>. The speed of light decreases in the denser medium.
  • → Case C: From Denser to Rarer Medium: When light travels from a denser medium to a rarer medium (e.g., glass to air), it bends away from the normal. <i is less than r>. The speed of light increases in the rarer medium.

Refraction Through Glass Slab

When light passes through a glass slab:

  • It bends towards the normal on entering (air → glass, denser medium).
  • It bends away from the normal on exiting (glass → air, rarer medium).
  • The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but slightly shifted sideways — this is called lateral displacement.

SPHERICAL LENSES

Spherical Lenses:

  • Spherical lenses are optical devices with curved, spherical surfaces that refract (bend) light, either converging or diverging it. They are classified into two main types: Convex (converging) and Concave (diverging) lens.
  • → Convex Lens: Centre bulged, ends narrow
  • → Concave Lens: Centre narrow, ends wider
  • → Convex Lens = Concave Mirror
  • → Concave Lens = Convex Mirror

Image Formation by Convex Lens

  • A convex lens (also called a converging lens) can form real or virtual images depending on the object's position.
Object PositionImage PositionNatureImage Size
At infinityAt focus (F)Real, invertedHighly diminished
Beyond 2FBetween F and 2FReal, invertedDiminished
At 2FAt 2FReal, invertedSame size
Between F and 2FBeyond 2FReal, invertedEnlarged
At focus (F)At infinityReal, invertedHighly enlarged
Between F and OOn same side of the lensVirtual, erectEnlarged

Image Formation by Concave Lens

  • A concave lens always forms a virtual, erect, and diminished image, regardless of the object's position.
Object PositionImage PositionNatureImage Size
At infinityAt FVirtual, erectHighly diminished
Between infinity and O (center)Between F and OVirtual, erectDiminished

Lens Formula: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f

  • f = Focal length of lens
  • v = Image distance from the lens
  • u = Object distance from the lens
Magnification (M) = -v/u
  • M = 1 (Image size = Object size)
  • M > 1 (Image is larger than object)
  • M < 1 (Image is smaller than object)

Uses of Lenses

  • Convex lens: Used in eyeglasses to correct hypermetropia (farsightedness), magnifying glasses, microscopes, cameras, telescopes.
  • Concave lens: Used in eyeglasses to correct myopia (nearsightedness).

Power of Lens

  • Power of a lens is the reciprocal of its focal length (in meters).
Power (P) = 100 / f(cm) = 1 / f(m)

S.I. Unit of Power

  • The SI unit of power is the dioptre (D) → 1 D = 1 m⁻¹.

Sign Convention

  • Convex lens (converging) → Positive power.
  • Concave lens (diverging) → Negative power.

Worked Example 1:

A concave lens has focal length of 15 cm. At what distance should the object from lens should be placed so that it forms an image at 10 cm from the lens? Also find the magnification of lens.

Sol: Given — Focal length, f = -15 cm (concave lens → focal length is negative); Image distance, v = -10 cm (virtual image formed on the same side as the object → also negative); Object distance, u = ?

Using 1/v - 1/u = 1/f: 1/(-10) - 1/u = 1/(-15) → 1/u = -1/10 + 1/15 → 1/u = -3/30 + 2/30 = -1/30 → u = -30

Magnification = hi/ho = v/u = -10/-30 = 1/3

This means the image is virtual, erect, and 1/3 the size of the object (diminished).

Worked Example 2:

If the focal length of a convex lens is 5cm, concave lens is 10 cm, and convex lens is 2 cm respectively. What power do we get after adding all the focal length?

Sol: Given — f of convex lens = +5 cm; f of concave lens = -10 cm; f of convex lens = +2 cm.

P₁ = 100/5 = +20 D; P₂ = 100/(-10) = -10 D; P₃ = 100/+2 = +50 D

P_total = P₁ + P₂ + P₃ = 20 + (-10) + 50 = 60 D

Diffraction

  • Diffraction is the bending or spreading of light (or any wave) around the edges of an obstacle or through a small opening.
  • Wide Gap: Small diffraction effect
  • Narrow Gap: Large diffraction effect
